title: Medium exam 1
about: Ten single-choice questions that combine two facts or ask you to trace two or three steps: modes, short pipelines, search order, argument counting and moving files.

questions.title: Reading a numeric mode
questions.text: `tool.sh` belongs to user `ana` and group `dev`, and its mode was set with `chmod 645 tool.sh`. Which statement is FALSE?

options.t: ana can read and modify the file, but cannot run it as `./tool.sh`.
options.why: True: the owner digit 6 is 4+2, that is `rw-`, with no execute bit.

options.t: A user who is not ana and is not in `dev` can read the file and run it as `./tool.sh`.
options.why: True: the last digit 5 is 4+1, that is `r-x`, for everybody else.

options.t: A member of `dev` (other than ana) can run it as `./tool.sh`, since "others" have execute.
options.why: False: a user is judged by one class only; a group member falls under the group digit 4 (`r--`), so he can read the file but gets "Permission denied" when running it. The "others" digit does not add to it.

options.t: A member of `dev` (other than ana) can read the file but cannot modify it.
options.why: True: the group digit 4 is `r--`.
That is the output of the first `tr` alone: the digits are deleted, but the double comma is still there until the second `tr` squeezes it.
The first `tr -d` deletes every digit, giving `a,b,,c`; then `tr -s ','` squeezes the repeated comma into one.
Squeezing (`-s`) collapses repeats into one character; it does not delete the commas (that would be `-d ','`).
That is what you would get from the squeeze alone; here the digits are deleted first.

questions.title: Picking fields by number
questions.text: The line `lucia:x:1004:1004:Lucia R:/home/lucia:/bin/zsh` follows the `/etc/passwd` layout. What does `echo '<that line>' | cut -d: -f7,3` print?

options.why: Field 3 is the UID and field 7 is the login shell; `cut` prints the selected fields in the order they appear in the line, whatever the order in the list.
`cut` never reorders fields: `-f7,3` is the same as `-f3,7`.
That would be `-f2,7`; field 2 is the password placeholder, not the UID.
The output is `1004:/bin/zsh`, which is one of the options above.

questions.title: Applying a changed GRUB setting
questions.text: On a Debian-based system you edited `GRUB_TIMEOUT` in `/etc/default/grub`. Which command makes GRUB use the new value at the next boot?

options.why: That writes the boot loader itself to the disk; it is not the step that regenerates the menu configuration.
`grub.cfg` is generated, not copied: `/etc/default/grub` is only the input of the generator and has a different format.
That rebuilds the initial RAM disk used by the kernel; it does not touch the GRUB configuration.
It regenerates `/boot/grub/grub.cfg` from `/etc/default/grub` and the scripts in `/etc/grub.d/`.

questions.title: Every match along the PATH
questions.text: Two directories, `/opt/a` and `/opt/b`, each contain an executable called `run`, and `PATH=/opt/b:/opt/a:/usr/bin:/bin`. Which command prints the full path of both of them, in the order the shell would find them?

options.why: It stops at the first match and prints only `/opt/b/run`.
`-a` lists all the matches along the `PATH`, here `/opt/b/run` and then `/opt/a/run`.
It only prints the `PATH` line if the text `run` appears in it, which it does not; it never looks inside the directories.
`$PATH` expands to the whole colon-separated string, so `ls` looks for one file with a very odd name and fails with "No such file or directory".

questions.title: Searching the manual pages
questions.text: Which statement about looking up manual pages is FALSE?

options.t: `whatis cp` prints the one-line description of each manual page named `cp`.
options.why: True: it is a lookup by name.

options.t: `apropos copy` can list `cp` even though `copy` is not its name.
options.why: True: it searches the descriptions as well, and `cp` is described as "copy files and directories".

options.t: `whatis copy` also lists `cp`, because its description contains the word `copy`.
options.why: False: `whatis` matches names only, and no page is called `copy`, so it answers `copy: nothing appropriate.`; the keyword search is `apropos copy` or `man -k copy`.

options.t: `man -k copy` performs the same search as `apropos copy`.
options.why: True: `-k` turns `man` into a keyword search.

questions.title: What a PID tells you
questions.text: Which statement about process identifiers is TRUE?

options.t: PIDs are handed out sequentially up to a maximum and then numbering starts again; PID 1 is the initial process that starts the services.
options.why: The number grows with each new process; the classic limit is 32767. PID 1 (nowadays usually systemd) is launched by the kernel at the end of its start-up.

options.t: A child process always gets the PID of its parent plus one, so `sleep 9 &` started from a shell with PID 500 is always PID 501.
options.why: Other processes may be created in between, and PIDs are not tied to the parent's number.

options.t: A PID belongs to a program, not to a running instance: `ls` always gets the same PID every time it runs.
options.why: Every execution is a new process with a new PID.

options.t: PID 1 is the login shell of the first user, created when that user authenticates.
options.why: PID 1 exists from boot, before any user logs in; a login shell has an ordinary PID.

questions.title: Counting the arguments
questions.text:
A script `t.sh` contains this function and these three calls:

```
count() { echo $#; }
count "$*"; count "$@"; count $*
```

You run `./t.sh "a b" c`. What does it print, one number per line?

options.why: `"$*"` is a single word joining all the arguments, so the first call receives 1 argument, not 2.
`"$@"` keeps the original boundaries: `a b` and `c` are 2 arguments.
Unquoted `$*` is split on blanks into `a`, `b` and `c`: 3 arguments.
`"$*"` is one word (`a b c`), `"$@"` keeps the two original arguments, and unquoted `$*` splits into three words.

questions.title: Moving into a directory
questions.text:
`docs` and `archive` are existing directories, and `notes` is a file, all in the current directory. You run:

```
mv notes docs/todo
mv docs archive
```

Where is the file now?

options.why: The first `mv` moves and renames the file in one step; the second one moves the directory `docs` into the existing directory `archive`.
`mv` does not merge: since `archive` is an existing directory, `docs` goes inside it as a whole.
The first command already renamed the file while moving it into `docs`: its name is `todo`.
The second command moved `docs` away: it no longer exists in the current directory.

questions.title: Removing something that is not there
questions.text: There is no file or directory called `ghost` in the current directory. Which statement is TRUE?
questions.note: `-f` does not make `rm` able to remove a directory without `-r`: `rm -f dir` still says "Is a directory". Use it with care: `-f` also hides mistakes.

options.t: `rm -r ghost` and `rm -rf ghost` both print the same error, because `-f` only skips the confirmation questions.
options.why: `-f` also ignores nonexistent files, so `rm -rf` stays silent.

options.t: `rm -ri ghost` asks "remove directory 'ghost'?" and then reports that it does not exist.
options.why: There is nothing to ask about: it reports the error straight away, as `rm -r` does.

options.t: `rm -r ghost` prints nothing and succeeds, because `-r` makes `rm` skip names that do not exist.
options.why: `-r` is about directories; a missing name is an error: "No such file or directory".

options.t: `rm -r ghost` prints "No such file or directory" and exits with status 1, while `rm -rf ghost` prints nothing and exits with status 0.
options.why: `-f` ignores nonexistent files and never prompts, which is why scripts use it.
